tone_statements.quote: I was not able to arrive at definite conclusions in regard to Haida stress and pitch and their interrelations. It is clear that a given word is regularly accented on a certain syllable. Generally this is the first [...] but the accented syllable does not need to be the first [...] Further, it is evident that the stressed syllable may lose its stress, as it reduces its quantity, in a given setting in the sentence or when the addition of one or more syllables changes the rhythmic pattern of its syllables. tone_statements.quote: I was not able to arrive at definite conclusions in regard to Haida stress and pitch and their interrelations. It is clear that a given word is regularly accented on a certain syllable. Generally this is the first, ... but the accented syllable does not need to be the first ... The question of stress is complicated by that of pitch. The stressed syllable is higher in pitch than the other syllables of the word. At the same time it seemed to me that a low-pitched syllable might very well bear a secondary stress so strong as to bring up the question whether, after all, what I have been making stress in this paper is not primarily a matter of relatively high pitch, only secondarily one of stress. Though I should not like to commit myself at present, I consider it very likely that pitch alternations are a primary factor in the dynamics of Haida ... If there are significant pitch alternations in Haida, they are probably of the simple Tlingit high-low type observed by Boas.

sources.citation: Hori, Hirofumi (堀博文). 2022. ハイダ語のピッチ付与規則について [Pitch Assignment Rules in Haida]. 静言論叢 (Seigen ronsō, Shizuoka University Linguistics Circle) 5: 125-146.
sources.note: Author's latest first-hand analysis, superseding Hori 1996/2001: every syllable carries one of two phonetic pitch levels [+H]/[-H], fully predictable from rhyme weight (bimoraic VV, VVC, VR -> [+H]; monomoraic V, VO -> [-H]); the earlier three-level H/M/L description (Hori 2001) is collapsed to two; pitch is 'phonetic, not phonological' (no lexical specification), functional load small, apparent pitch minimal pairs (e.g. 'eagle' vs 'box') derived from underlying mora count plus a morphologically conditioned vowel-lengthening rule; explicitly leaves open whether to call the system tone, pitch…

tone.quote: p.125 §1: 「ハイダ語の韻律的特徴として，音声的な声の高さであるピッチが個々の音節に現われる点があげられる 1。そのピッチは，大まかにいえば，高ピッチ（[+H]と表記する）と非高ピッチ（[ − H] と表記する）の二種類があるが，そのいずれが現われるかは，音節構造から予測することができる。」 [...] p.146, English abstract: "It is revealed that the occurrences of each pitch can be predicted from the syllable structure: if the rhyme of a syllable is bimoraic (i.e., /VV/, /VVC/, and /VR/, where /R/ includes /m, n, ŋ, w, y, l/), it is assigned [+H]; if the syllable is monomoraic (i.e., /V/ and /VO/, where /O/ includes an obstruent), it is assigned [ − H]."
tone.locator: p.125 section 1 はじめに; p.146 English abstract; rules restated as (24)-(25) p.142
tone.translation: p.125: 'A prosodic characteristic of Haida is that pitch, i.e. phonetic voice height, appears on each individual syllable. Broadly speaking there are two kinds of pitch, high pitch (written [+H]) and non-high pitch (written [-H]), but which of them appears can be predicted from the syllable structure.' (abstract sentence is already English)

sources.citation: Hori, Hirofumi (堀博文). 2001. ハイダ語(北米インディアン諸語)の声調について [On tone in Haida (North American Indian languages)] (特集: 世界の声調・アクセント言語 [Special issue: Tone and accent languages of the world]). 音声研究 (Journal of the Phonetic Society of Japan) 5(1): 28-36.
sources.note: English abstract (read on J-STAGE): Haida 'has three levels of phonetic tone, namely high (H), mid (M), and low (L), whose occurrences correlate with the syllable structure and the morphological process'; distributions in mono- and polysyllabic words; argues tones 'are not specified in the underlying level but are predictable from the syllable structure and certain morphological information' and postulates tone assignment rules. Dedicated tone paper in a tone/accent special issue; not downloaded (one-download rule; 2022 paper supersedes it).
sources.venue: 音声研究 (Journal of the Phonetic Society of Japan)
